title: ‘Save the World Cup’: Trio of bills proposed to limit ICE involvement at matches in U.S.
content:
A New Jersey congresswoman has introduced a bill requesting that no federal funding should be used to carry out immigration enforcement activity within one mile of any FIFA World Cup match or Fan Festival during the tournament in the United States this summer.

The Athletic has seen and reviewed a draft of the bill, titled the “Save the World Cup Act”. Rep. Nellie Pou (D-N.J.) is the author of the proposed legislation, which has also been co-sponsored by Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) and Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-CA)

It is one of a package of three bills that the three members of Congress have introduced relating to the World Cup. Swalwell has authored a bill entitled the “Safe Passage to the World Cup” act, which seeks to prevent federal funds being used to carry out immigration enforcement on public transit or at public transits in any U.S. metropolitan area hosting a World Cup match or FIFA Fan Festival during the entirety of the tournament. Pou and McIver are original co-sponsors of the bill.

Swalwell and Pou have then acted as co-sponsors of McIver’s “Protect the World Cup attendees” proposal, which seeks to prevent agencies or entities that have taken federal money from participating in immigration enforcement programs during the World Cup. This would include entities such as police forces who have taken 287(g) agreements with the federal government, which essentially allow ICE to deputize local police to enforce civil immigration. Many World Cup host cities are not subject to these agreements, but there are high-profile cases, including sheriff’s offices in Miami-Dade County, Florida, which is home to Hard Rock Stadium, and Tarrant County in Texas, home to AT&T Stadium.

Of the 104 World Cup matches this summer, 78 will be held in the U.S. with 13 each in Canada and Mexico.

Pou, Swalwell and McIver are all Democrat members on the House Homeland Security Task Force, which helps to oversee and scrutinize World Cup security. Pou also represents New Jersey’s 9th district, which includes East Rutherford’s MetLife Stadium, the site of eight World Cup matches including the final.

Pou previously attracted headlines when she questioned the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) interim director Todd Lyons at a committee hearing last month. Lyons was testifying before members of the U.S. House of Representatives for the first time since government agents shot and killed two Minnesotans, Alex Pretti and Renee Good. Pou asked Lyons to commit to pausing ICE operations during the World Cup but Lyons did not do so, instead insisting the agency would play a “key part” in ensuring security.

He said ICE’s primary role, as is common at sporting events, would center on Homeland Security investigations, but Rep. Pou says she remains concerned that the involvement of ICE may lead people to fear immigration enforcement raids close to World Cup events.

Last summer, FIFA was alerted to human rights complaints by fans during the Club World Cup, which included alleged sightings of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officials and ICE officials at stadiums during the tournament. In a statement to The Athletic in September, a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson said that despite the reports made to FIFA, neither ICE nor CPB conducted enforcement, describing it as “another case of fear-mongering.”

Pou’s bill proposes congressional limitations on ICE activity during the World Cup. The bill proposes that “no Federal funds made available to the Department of Homeland Security or Department of Justice may be used to carry out any civil immigration enforcement activity within one mile of any 2026 FIFA World Cup match or Fan Festival, and for other purposes.”

The Athletic asked Pou how a limitation on ICE activity within a mile of official Fan Festivals or games would work. She said it should be for the duration of the tournament, rather than only on game-days. She also said she did not wish to prevent legitimate and necessary ICE activity. “It needs to be done in a manner that does not create unnecessary fear and concern to those attending the games,” Pou told The Athletic.

“The games are less than 90 days away from happening and given we still do not know what the immigration director Mr. Lyons is going to do, I want to make sure that we have legislation that clearly points out the parameters that must be taken into account. The timing of this is appropriate and one for us to really consider doing.”

She added that she has “pressed FIFA for assurance” that there would be no ICE raids at or near the stadiums but, she added, “we have not received any communication or confirmation to that effect.” FIFA declined to comment.

Rep. McIver, a co-sponsor of the bill, has been a vocal critic of ICE activity under the Trump administration. She was charged with assaulting law enforcement officers outside an ICE detention facility in New Jersey last May. She had been in attendance to make an oversight visit when the incident occurred amid a scrum as officers attempted to arrest the Mayor of Newark Ras Baraka. McIver was accused of using her forearms to strike two officers.

A spokesperson for McIver told The Athletic she will appeal the charges against her, claiming a congressional immunity clause which she claims may protect her against prosecution. In a statement, McIver said: “Legislative immunity doesn’t put members of Congress above the law, it protects the public’s right to have a voice — especially when that voice challenges power. I can’t, and won’t, back down — that’s what this appeal is about. I will keep challenging power, demanding oversight … the community that sent me to Congress to act as their voice cannot be silenced by this administration.”

While Democrats are introducing the bill, Rep. Pou says she “hopes” Republicans will also “take this matter very seriously.” She added: “I believe there are many that are going to do that. I just don’t think that we should just stand idly by and see what ICE does. We need to take action. It can certainly be via this bill.”

At the least, Pou says, she wants to “begin conversations.”

In a statement about his bill to limit ICE activity on public transport during the World Cup, Swalwell said: “As a former Division 1 soccer player, I know what an honour it is to host the world’s biggest sporting event. Our priority should be to showcase our best, not have police commandeering buses, trains and public spaces. This bill ensures ICE cannot turn everyday public transportation into a place of terror.”

A spokesperson for the DHS insisted to The Athletic that the mission of the agency is to “ensure every fan — Americans and visitors alike — has a safe and unforgettable experience”, adding that they wish to “showcase American greatness to the entire world.”

They continued: “DHS will work with our local and federal partners to secure the 2026 FIFA World Cup — in line with federal law, the U.S. Constitution — as we do with every major sporting event.

“International visitors who legally come to the United States for the World Cup have nothing to worry about. What makes someone a target for immigration enforcement is whether or not they are illegally in the U.S. — full stop. Speculation to the contrary is ill-informed. At the same time, foreign visitors MUST be proactive and should start working on their travel plans and documents well ahead of time to ensure a smooth travel experience.”

The build-up to this World Cup has been dominated by discussions relating to domestic politics in the United States and geopolitics across the world. Four participating countries — Iran, Haiti, Senegal and Ivory Coast — remain subject to travel bans, impacting the ability of their fans to attend the tournament, while the U.S. is also now embroiled in a conflict with the Iranian regime, leading to uncertainty over the country’s involvement in the World Cup. Pou, however, says she is focused on reducing risks around what she deems to be the threat on U.S. soil.

She says: “There’s no successful World Cup when fans and players are afraid of being wrongfully detained or swept up in an immigration raid. I refuse to allow this once-in-a-generation opportunity to be sabotaged by fear or reckless enforcement.

“This is an opportunity for our country to really showcase what we can do. I strongly believe we have the capability of doing that, and my goals are to provide peace of mind and protect our visitors, our residents and our players.”
